findings.claim: Functionalism represents the consensus view; Marxism, feminism and the New Right each offer different conflict analyses.
findings.truth: The New Right is not a conflict perspective. It shares functionalism's support for the traditional nuclear family and adds a political criticism of family change. The same lesson says exactly that three paragraphs later, and the lesson's own tooltip defines conflict perspectives as Marxism and feminism.
findings.evidence: spec 2.4 lists 'consensus view of Functionalism', 'conflict view of Marxism', 'conflict view of Feminism', then 'New Right views of family' as a separate bullet; internal contradiction with the L4 New Right section and L4 flashcard 10

findings.claim: By the mid-1990s this had risen to around 175,000 per year.
findings.truth: Divorces in England and Wales have never reached 175,000 in any year. The all-time high was 1993 at about 165,000; the mid-1990s years ran at roughly 155,000 to 158,000.
findings.evidence: ONS 'Divorces in England and Wales' bulletins (2016, 2018, 2019) call 2003 the most recent peak and put 2019 (107,599 divorces) 30% below it, so the 2003 peak was about 153,000 and the earlier 1990s high was well under 175,000

findings.claim: The mark scheme explicitly rewards candidates who present the functionalist case AND at least two contrasting perspectives.
findings.truth: No mark scheme is quoted in the spec and none was available to the lesson. The advice itself is sound, but it must not be presented as a mark-scheme instruction.
findings.evidence: spec section 3.1 prints only the assessment objectives and their weightings; house rule on copyright distancing and fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: the examiners reward answers that present the feminist critique
findings.truth: A fabricated examiner claim. The same advice reads correctly as a statement about what a top-band answer contains.
findings.evidence: spec section 3.1; house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: The tooltip on the word 'patriarchal' reads: "Delphy and Leonard's term for a family structure in which the husband is the head and chief beneficiary, and women's labour is systematically appropriated for his benefit."
findings.truth: Patriarchy is not a term coined by Delphy and Leonard, and the tooltip does not define the word the student clicked. Patriarchy is a system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions including the family.
findings.evidence: the glossary entries for 'patriarchy' in this lesson and in L5 already give the correct definition

findings.truth: The 'connected family' is not an established sociological term. The nearest real concepts are the networked family (Rainie and Wellman) and Smart's 'connectedness' in the personal life perspective. Neither is named here, so the phrase reads as key terminology that does not exist.
findings.evidence: not present in the spec; no sociologist is named in the lesson

findings.claim: Oakley developed the concept of the double shift (repeated in L4, L5 and L6, in L3 knowledge check 2, and in the L3 glossary).
findings.truth: Two defensible options. (a) Leave it: UK GCSE resources routinely attach the 'dual burden' or 'double shift' to Oakley (1974), and an answer saying 'Oakley: double shift' would be credited, so no marks are at risk. (b) Tighten it: 'second shift' was coined by Hochschild (1989) and 'triple shift' by Duncombe and Marsden (1995); Oakley (1974) evidenced the unequal domestic division of labour rather than naming the term. Option (b) touches content_html in four lessons, one knowledge check stem, one glossary entry and several mark schemes. Recommendation: leave.
findings.evidence: spec 2.4 names Oakley and the conventional family only; Hochschild, The Second Shift, 1989; Oakley, The Sociology of Housework, 1974
findings.ruling: NOTE: 'double shift' attributed to Oakley is standard GCSE usage; no marks at risk; left.

findings.claim: The Civil Partnership Act 2004 and the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 gave same-sex couples in the UK formal legal recognition.
findings.truth: The Civil Partnership Act 2004 was UK-wide, but the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 covers England and Wales only (in force 13 March 2014). Scotland legislated separately in 2014 and Northern Ireland in 2020. No date in the lesson is wrong, so the wording is loose rather than false.
findings.evidence: legislation.gov.uk, extent of the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013

findings.claim: The nuclear family remains the most common form according to ONS data.
findings.truth: True of families with dependent children, not of all families. ONS 2022: 19.4 million families, of which 42% (8.2 million) have dependent children, so couple-with-dependent-children families are about a third of all families; married or civil partner couple families (12.7 million, 65%) are the largest ONS category. The claim is standard GCSE shorthand and would be credited, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: ONS, Families and households in the UK: 2022 (12.7m married couple, 3.6m cohabiting, 2.9m lone parent families)

findings.claim: In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare - around 25,000 divorces per year in England and Wales.
findings.truth: About 25,000 to 30,000 a year describes the 1950s baseline, not the whole decade after 1945: divorces spiked to roughly 60,000 in 1947 as wartime marriages ended. Not edited because the annual series could not be confirmed from an official page in this session.
findings.evidence: ONS historical divorce series (the bulletins reachable as text carry no pre-1970 figures)

findings.claim: Ann Oakley and other feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a manifestation of patriarchal power relations (L5 knowledge check 1 makes Oakley the answer).
findings.truth: The canonical study is Dobash and Dobash (1979); Oakley's own research is on housework and gender roles. No study, title or figure is invented here and the claim is perspective-level, so the knowledge check stays answerable (Oakley is the only feminist among the options).
findings.evidence: spec 2.4 names only Delphy and Leonard and Oakley for feminism; Dobash and Dobash, Violence Against Wives, 1979

findings.claim: Question tariffs quoted across all six lessons: 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and 12-mark questions, and 'one mark per described cause'.
findings.truth: The spec prints no question ladder, so these tariffs cannot be verified. Nothing in the unit contradicts the facts the spec does print: a 1 hour 45 minute written exam, 100 marks, 50% of the qualification, AO1 40 / AO2 40 / AO3 20, and at least 15% of marks for research methods. No 20 or 25-mark question, no SPaG claim and no other board's paper names appear anywhere in the unit.
findings.evidence: spec summary of assessment and section 3.1

summary: Six lessons checked. Sociologist attributions, dates, Acts, statistics and all 30 knowledge check answer keys are otherwise sound. Six fixes: the New Right taught as a conflict perspective (HIGH), an impossible divorce figure of 175,000 a year (HIGH), two fabricated examiner or mark-scheme claims, a wrong tooltip definition of 'patriarchal', and an invented term ('the connected family'). One item for Tom: whether to keep the standard GCSE attribution of the double shift to Oakley. No board name appears in any student-facing prose.
